native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: HYPOTHESIS: Median family net wealth in the NLSY79 cohort shows persistent and substantial racial/ethnic gaps from 1985 through 1996. Wealth is measured at the family (household) level, not per individual. In 1985, the median family net wealth was $3,500 for non-Black, non-Hispanic respondents (n=5774), $1,600 for Black respondents (n=1699), and $500 for Hispanic respondents (n=2631). The non-Black, non-Hispanic median exceeded the Black median by $1,900 (2.2×) and the Hispanic median by $3,000 (7.0×). By 1990, medians had risen across all groups: $12,972 (non-Black, non-Hispanic, n=5336), $4,800 (Black, n=1528), and $1,600 (Hispanic, n=2431). The gaps persisted: the non-Black, non-Hispanic median was $8,172 (2.7×) above the Black median and $11,372 (8.1×) above the Hispanic median. By 1996, medians had increased further: $42,600 (non-Black, non-Hispanic, n=3557), $9,800 (Black, n=1368), and $2,562 (Hispanic, n=2114). The non-Black, non-Hispanic median remained $32,800 (4.3×) above the Black median and $40,038 (16.6×) above the Hispanic median. Sensitivity check (matched cohort): Restricting to the 5739 respondents with non-missing wealth in all three waves, the gap direction and rough magnitude hold. The 1985 non-Black, non-Hispanic vs. Black gap is $2,200 (vs. $1,900 in the full sample, +15.8%); the 1996 gap is $33,525 (vs. $32,800, +2.2%). The Hispanic gaps show a similar pattern (+16.7% in 1985, +0.4% in 1996). The matched-cohort gaps are in the same direction and of comparable magnitude, supporting the robustness of the main findings despite differential attrition. Direction of change: Median family net wealth increased across all three groups from 1985 to 1996, consistent with cohort aging and general wealth accumulation. The absolute gaps between the non-Black, non-Hispanic group and both the Black and Hispanic groups widened over this period, while the ratio gaps remained substantial throughout. The non-Black, non-Hispanic group maintained the highest median family net wealth at every time point. Limitations: (1) The 'non-Black, non-Hispanic' category (code 3) is used as a proxy for 'white' individuals; it includes Asian, Native American, and other races, so the reported gaps are 'non-Black, non-Hispanic vs. Black/Hispanic,' not strictly 'white vs. Black/Hispanic.' (2) Wealth is measured at the family (household) level, not per individual; family net wealth is not equivalent to per-person wealth. (3) The three time points (1985, 1990, 1996) are discrete cross-sections, not a continuous trend; we characterize direction of change between them but cannot model a trajectory. (4) Missingness increases substantially across waves (20.4% in 1985, 26.7% in 1990, 44.5% in 1996) and is differential by race — the non-Black, non-Hispanic group has the highest missingness in every wave (52.6% by 1996 vs. 31.7% for Black). The non-missing sample composition shifts across waves, which could bias the 1996 comparison. The matched-cohort sensitivity check (n=5,739) shows the gaps are directionally stable under this restriction. (5) No sampling weights were available; results are unweighted sample medians, not population estimates.
